turn_text: This is Fusion Capitalism. A clean energy vision for conservatives. Brought to you by industry leader and company CEO Steve Malek. Here's Steve.

Joining me this week is Congressman Scott Peters, who serves California's 52nd Congressional District, which includes the cities of Coronado, Palway, and most of Northern San Diego. First elected in 2012, he currently serves on the House Small Business Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee. Representative Peters, welcome to the podcast.

It's my pleasure to have you. Congressman, to provide our audience with some initial background, you've been ranked as high as the fourth most independent Democrat in Congress. Why do you feel this is a significant accomplishment?

Well, you know, my orientation about solving problems is that we're best off if we do it together as a country. I don't know that We can ever say we've won a world war or gone to the moon or done anything ambitious with one political party. So I just think it's important to be listening for solutions that make sense for the whole country. And that's through bipartisanship.

And to provide more of that context, before Congress and serving on the San Diego City Council, you worked as an economist at the Environmental Protection Agency. Can you tell us where your interest and passion for the environment came from?

When I got out of college, I was thinking about whether it become an economist or a lawyer, frankly. And the job I got was being an economist at the United States Environmental Protection Agency. It was a low-level economics job. But we were looking at the effect of new chemicals, whether new chemicals should be regulated. And I got a taste for how that kind of worked from the inside. The thing I noticed from a career perspective is that no one really listened to the economists and everyone listened to the lawyers. So I ended up going to law school. When I got out, I was at a large firm at the dawn of the cleanup area under the Superfund law, the Circla law, and I was working in the Midwest, and my firm had a lot of clients that had legacy manufacturing facilities. They hadn't done anything wrong under the law back then, but Circla imposed this retroactive liability on them. So we had a lot of amazing environmental cleanups that we had to conduct, and I just got the bug for it. a little bit of litigation because you were fighting over how much each company would pay to do a particular cleanup. But it was also interesting to work on those technical issues. So that was kind of my legal career. That led naturally to an interest in policy as I was involved in. As I moved transition from being strictly a lawyer who was interested in politics to a politician who thought like solving problems like a lawyer.

turn_text: I'd like to split this podcast into two sections, the first section being that we focus on the problem of climate change, a problem that's garnering more and more concern across our country and around the world. But then in the second part, I'd like to focus on the solution to this problem, which I think is increasingly being seen as a tremendous opportunity. So going back to the problem, can you tell us, I'm just curious, being in the House of Representatives, are your conservative brethren as passionate in their disbelief in climate change in private as they are in public?

No, and I think that's waning to be honest with you. The issue is not so much that people deny the science of climate change anymore, although clearly, the senator held up a snowball in the Senate as evidence that there wasn't global warming. I mean, you still do get that. But I think, increasingly, there's a recognition that the accumulation of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and the short-term climate pollutants like methane and hydrofluorocarbons are causing changes, and people are seeing them. And I think that's what's happening. People on the ground are seeing things being different. And in Republican areas, farmers are having a difficult time dealing with these changes. You see from a foreign policy perspective that the military is warning us about mass migrations and more violence resulting from sea level rise. Syria has a lot to do with the climatic changes that help people not get food. And so I think it's harder and harder to deny that this is happening. Miami has wet streets on sunny days. Now the issue is how do they enter the politics of this? Because the hard thing is that this is going to cause a lot of disruption for people at home. If you're in Texas and you hear about climate change, voters think, well, I'm going to lose my job. And a lot of people who are involved in extraction industries in Texas, Oklahoma, West Virginia. The first thing they want to think about is feeding their family this month. They're not worried about what the world's going to be like in 50 years. So the issue is how do we make this transition in a way that really appreciates the dislocations that are going to happen and deals with them while taking advantage of the opportunities that are headed for the country?

turn_text: It seems there is a more consensus around the solution than the problem, as we've discussed. And I think that's largely because of the economic opportunities of clean energy. For example, I've read that Texas now has more jobs in the clean energy industry than in the fossil fuel industry. And I understand that you've developed a climate playbook. And so can you tell us more about that and maybe address the economic opportunities of addressing the problem?

The concept of the climate playbook is to get away from talking about what's wrong to what we can do about it. And so, you know, we've got a lot of ideas for decarbonizing the economy, taking carbon dioxide out of energy production, transportation, agriculture, buildings, industry, and there's various strategies you would do across each of those. We've got to come up with research on new technologies. We've got to invest in research on new technologies. We've got to look at carbon capture technologies that would draw carbon back from the atmosphere. Some of those could be natural, like trees and restoration of natural systems in the ocean. Some of those could be engineered, like direct air capture. We've got to look at a pricing mechanism for carbon so that we send the right price signals to the economy. And then we've got to deal with short-lived climate pollutants. And at the same time, We do all that mitigation. We've got to deal with adaptation. We've got to get ready for the effects of climate change that we know are coming, whether those are intense different periods of drought, sea level rise, or whatever those might be. There's a lot of jobs opportunities in those things. It's true. This is not a jobs program, but there's going to be a lot of investment. And then I think the other orientation we have to have is that it's as taxpayers, it's much more expensive to wait till this happens to us. for us to invest now and get ahead of it. So very much like COVID, if you just spend a little bit of money on preventing COVID, you could have saved a ton of money in responding to it. Climate's going to be that many, many times over. So the idea of the climate playbook is let's figure out all these actions we have to take. Every congressional committee has essentially has a role, whether you're talking about agriculture or tax breaks at ways and means or you know, regulating oil and gas at energy and commerce, but we need to get working on it. That's the idea of trying to force action through a playbook.
